name: RegiÃ³n de ValparaÃ­so
summary:
In 2024 Valparaíso concentrated 51.32 % of all national anti-LGBTI discrimination cases recorded by Movilh — more than twice the share of the second-placed Región Metropolitana (25.12 %) — after an 80.93 % year-on-year increase over 2023. It is the single largest regional outlier in the Chilean dataset and the only region where over half of the country's documented homo/transphobic incidents fall. In 2025, Valparaíso and Metropolitana were the only two regions where recorded cases fell, while all fourteen others rose; Movilh reads this not as improvement but as the decentralisation of hate toward territories with less LGBTIQ+ visibility, meaning the underlying pressure did not abate — it dispersed.

Against the national score of 0.72, this is a −0.16 deviation, the largest in the country. Chile's legal framework (Gender Identity Law 21.120, anti-discrimination law 21.220) is identical here; the deviation is entirely a volume-of-incident finding. For a visitor to Valparaíso or Viña del Mar, the probability of encountering hostile environments — verbal harassment, refusal of service, workplace-style discrimination — is materially and repeatedly higher than anywhere else in Chile.

Compared with the next-worst unit, Bío-Bío (0.62), Valparaíso's −0.06 additional gap reflects not a specific institutional failure but sheer case concentration: Bío-Bío's finding is one hospital placement and a municipal office dismantling, while Valparaíso carries over half the national case load. Compared with Magallanes (0.66), which has a violent-crime and sentencing story, Valparaíso's problem is systemic density of low-to-mid-severity incidents rather than isolated severity.

name: RegiÃ³n del BÃ­o-BÃ­o
summary:
Movilh-Biobío formally denounced what it called "brutal and illegal acts of discrimination" at the Hospital Traumatológico de Concepción, where a trans woman was placed in men's beds in contravention of Law 21.120 and public health policy requiring treatment by chosen name and social sex. The complaint was lodged with the Seremi de Salud. This is the closest Chilean analogue to a facility-misassignment incident directly encountered by a visitor: an emergency-room or inpatient visit in Bío-Bío carries a documented risk of gender-mismatched placement. Separately, Concepción's municipality dismissed the staff of its Oficina de la Diversidad y No Discriminación during January 2025 honourary-staff cuts, which LGBTIQA+ organisations called a "dismantling" leaving one person in post.

Bío-Bío held 5.89 % of the national case total in 2024 — third highest — reinforcing that the region's institutional failures occur against an elevated baseline of discrimination reports. Against the national 0.72, this is a −0.10 deviation driven by two concrete traveler-facing findings: the hospital bed placement (medical exposure) and the diversity-office dismantling (loss of local complaint infrastructure).

Compared with Valparaíso (0.56), Bío-Bío is 0.06 higher: Valparaíso's problem is the volume of over half the national case load, while Bío-Bío has specific institutional incidents but a normalised share. Compared with Tarapacá (0.64), Bío-Bío is 0.02 lower: Tarapacá's finding is a judicial annulment that devalues trans life in theory, whereas Bío-Bío's hospital episode shows how that devaluation manifests in the care a visitor might actually receive.

name: RegiÃ³n de TarapacÃ¡
summary:
The Court of Appeals of Iquique annulled the entire trial over the killing of a transgender woman, holding that Chile's "femicide" (femicidio) offence — the strongest gendered-violence protection in the penal code — covers only "a person biologically female" and therefore the conviction could not stand as framed. This is a named judicial finding that, in this region, the most severe legal protection available for gender-motivated violence does not extend to trans women. The annulment occurred in Tarapacá, where the Iquique court exercises jurisdiction. Tarapacá accounted for 1.56 % of the national anti-LGBTI case total in 2024, a small-share region in which a single structural finding dominates the per-capita signal.

Against the national 0.72, this is a −0.08 deviation. The legal framework is unchanged (Law 21.120 and the femicide article remain on the books nationally), but the regional judiciary's operative interpretation in this instance creates a concrete protection gap for a trans person who is assaulted in Tarapacá. Compared with La Araucanía (0.65), Tarapacá is 0.01 lower: Araucanía's −0.07 is trend-based (+150 % rise, low visibility), whereas Tarapacá carries a specific court ruling that names trans women as outside the femicide definition.

Compared with Arica y Parinacota (0.69), Tarapacá is 0.05 lower because the Iquique annulment is a documented finding within Tarapacá's own judicial district, whereas Arica's deviation rests on the shared northern-court context with no trans-specific incident of its own.

name: RegiÃ³n de La AraucanÃ­a
summary:
Movilh's XXIV annual report (March 2026) identifies La Araucanía as the region where reported homo/transphobic cases rose most sharply in 2025 — up approximately 150 % year-on-year — during a year when the national total hit a record 3,620 documented cases (+27.1 %). The region's formal trans visibility is extremely low: only 157 people used the Gender Identity Law (21.120) for name and legal-sex rectification in its first three years, indicating a community with minimal institutional presence. Movilh interprets the pattern as the decentralisation of hate toward territories where LGBTIQ+ themes have less public debate, stating this "appears aimed at obstructing" equality work.

Against the national 0.72, this is a −0.07 deviation, trend-driven rather than incident-specific. There is no trans-specific Mapuche customary-law jurisdiction or documented state-implicated violence in the dossier; the indigenous-note is structural context within a region under prolonged security conflict. Compared with Tarapacá (0.64), La Araucanía is 0.01 higher: Tarapacá carries a concrete judicial annulment, whereas Araucanía's finding is a statistical acceleration from a low base. Compared with Valparaíso (0.56), it is 0.09 higher despite the 150 % rise, because Araucanía's absolute share (0.72 % of national cases) remains marginal.

For a visitor, the practical implication is not a specific hostile incident but the trajectory: the fastest-rising region with the thinnest LGBTI support infrastructure and least public visibility means fewer allies, fewer complaint channels, and a deteriorating climate without institutional counterweight.

name: RegiÃ³n de Magallanes y AntÃ¡rtica Chilena
summary:
In 2024 a trans woman, Kenia Chacón, was the victim of an attempted femicide (femicidio frustrado) in Punta Arenas. The tribunal imposed four years of internación parcial against the five years of internación total requested by the prosecution; the victim's mother publicly denounced devaluation of the attack on the basis of her daughter's gender identity. In April 2026 the regional director of SernamEG (the national women and gender-equality service) publicly criticised the sentence as not reflecting the gravity of the attack and announced an appeal — a named institutional pushback that partially offsets the judicial under-penalisation. Magallanes also appeared among the regions with the largest percentage increases in the 2024 dataset and holds 0.96 % of the national case total.

Against the national 0.72, this is a −0.06 deviation. The under-sentencing for gender-motivated violence against a trans woman is a concrete traveler-relevant severity finding; the SernamEG appeal is a genuine institutional counter-signal that prevents a deeper deduction. Compared with Tarapacá (0.64), Magallanes is 0.02 higher: Tarapacá's Iquique court annulment voids the femicide protection entirely for trans women in that jurisdiction, whereas Magallanes applied the femicide framework but under-sentenced, and the state service is actively appealing to correct the record.

For a visitor, the practical exposure in Magallanes is low absolute case volume (0.96 % of the national total) but the judicial precedent of reduced sentences for attacks on trans women is a severity signal that moves the region below national.

name: RegiÃ³n de Ãuble
summary:
Ñuble registered a 300 % increase in recorded homo/transphobic cases in 2024, the sharpest percentage rise of any Chilean region, though from an extremely small base: Ñuble held only 1.44 % of the national case total. La Discusión's reporting of two historic gender-identity rectification cases in Ñuble illustrates how minimal the formal trans presence is in the region. The statistical alarm is real — the fastest percentage growth in the country — but the absolute numbers remain marginal, and no region-specific legal finding, institutional incident, or enforcement failure was identified in the dossier beyond the case-volume trend.

Against the national 0.72, this is a −0.05 deviation, driven entirely by the rate-of-change signal. Compared with Bío-Bío (0.62), which is 0.05 lower, Ñuble lacks the hospital bed-placement and diversity-office-dismantling findings that give Bío-Bío a concrete traveler-facing institutional failure. Ñuble's evidence is statistical trajectory without a named incident. Compared with La Araucanía (0.65), Ñuble is 0.02 higher: Araucanía's +150 % is in the most recent year (2025) and is accompanied by the lowest gender-identity-law uptake of any region (157 in three years), painting a more sustained picture of emerging hostility with no institutional counterweight.

name: RegiÃ³n de Arica y Parinacota
summary:
Arica y Parinacota is grouped with Tarapacá in the dossier under the heading "the northern courts' non-recognition of trans women as women," reflecting the shared judicial geography of northern Chile. However, the specific Iquique Court of Appeals annulment was delivered in Tarapacá, and Arica's own data contribution is limited to a 0.84 % share of national cases (2024). No trans-specific incident, court ruling, or enforcement failure originating in Arica was identified. The deviation below national rests on the shared northern judicial-climate framing and the broader pattern that all fourteen regions outside Valparaíso and Metropolitana saw cases rise in 2025.

Against the national 0.72, this is a −0.03 deviation, the smallest in the scored set. Compared with Tarapacá (0.64), Arica is 0.05 higher because it lacks the concrete femicide-annulment ruling; the northern-court context applies but is not evidenced with a named local finding. Compared with Ñuble (0.67), Arica is 0.02 higher: Ñuble's +300 % surge is a more specific and dramatic statistical signal than Arica's sub-percent case share.

For a visitor, the practical exposure in Arica is not materially different from the national baseline; the small deduction reflects the dossier's explicit grouping under "worse than national" and the absence of any positive institutional finding (no diversity office, no municipal ordinance, no documented court protection).

name: RegiÃ³n Metropolitana de Santiago
summary:
Metropolitana is the region of best and worst in the country compressed into one administrative unit. Ñuñoa approved the first municipal anti-discrimination ordinance in Chile that explicitly prohibits hate speech, obliges non-discrimination clauses in municipal tenders and contracts, creates a communal seal for good practice, and requires anti-exclusion notices in municipal buildings — a genuinely first-in-country institutional protection for a visitor in that commune. Vitacura's mayor declined to raise the LGBT pride flag on 17 May after a rebellion by Republican councillors, despite a prior commitment to Movilh. The ADM1 unit's internal spread (Ñuñoa vs Vitacura) is larger than most regions' entire deviation from the national score.

Metropolitana held 25.12 % of national cases in 2024 (second only to Valparaíso), but as the country's most populous region this share is roughly proportional. In 2025, Metropolitana was one of only two regions where recorded cases fell. The unit carries the strongest institutional depth in Chile: national-level courts, the largest civil-society infrastructure, the greatest concentration of trans and non-binary community resources, and the highest density of legal aid and complaint mechanisms available to a visitor who encounters discrimination.

Against the national 0.72, this is a +0.02 deviation, the only positive unit score. The Ñuñoa ordinance and the falling case count edge the region slightly above national; the Vitacura episode and the 25 % share pull the other way but are offset by proportional population. Compared with Valparaíso (0.56), the +0.18 gap reflects that Santiago, despite carrying a quarter of national cases, has the institutional machinery to respond, while Valparaíso's problem is density of incidents without equivalent counterweight.
